rejected.title: Representation of people, places and events
card: Representation is the way a text shows a person, place or event. It is a version of that subject, not the whole truth.
Every text leaves things out and puts other things in focus. The writer or maker chooses which details, words and images to use.
The version also reflects when, where and by whom the text was made. A text made in another time or place, or by someone with a different view, can show the same subject differently.
To read a representation, ask what is included, what is left out, and who made the text and why.
rejected.remember: A text gives one version of its subject, shaped by who made it, and when and where.

a.q: A tourist brochure shows only sunny beaches and smiling locals in a seaside town. What does this show about representation?
opts: It gives one chosen version of the town
It gives the whole truth about the town
It shows the town as it is in every season
It shows how locals would describe the town
a.why: The brochure's makers chose which details to include, so it presents a version of the town. It is not the whole truth, because it leaves out other sides of the place.
a.clue: Think about what the brochure chose to show and leave out.

b.q: A newspaper in 1920 and a website today both report on the same town flood. Their reports describe the event quite differently. What is the best reason?
opts: Each report reflects the time it was made and who made it
The 1920 report is true, as it was written at the time
The website report is true, as it can use more sources
The flood changed, so the later report shows a new event
b.why: Representations are shaped by the time, place and maker of a text, so two texts about one event can differ. It is tempting to think one report is simply the true one, but each is a version that leaves things out, so neither is the whole truth.
b.clue: Neither report is the whole truth. What shapes each version?
